<document>
# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
I've read it. Here's what it reports, then where it holds, where it slips, and how it changes the picture.

## Restatement

This is a registered 24-month follow-up of two sources. The protocol was filed at month 11, before outcomes were available.

**Varden case-processing (7 v 7 offices):**

| Measure | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% | +9.8% |
| Output per hour, system logs (new measure) | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Output per FTE | −2.1% | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |

- Quality is unchanged, sick days are still down 27%, and resignations remain lower.
- A registered mediation analysis attributes 47% of the per-hour gain to fewer recurring meetings (CI 28–66), 18% to reduced fatigue (CI 2–34), and leaves 35% unexplained.
- Two control offices ran their own "meeting audit" in month 15 without changing hours. Their output per hour rose 4.1% against their own previous six months.

**Varden counter offices:** the county ended this arm at month 12. Waits were 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and restoring service would have needed 12% more staff, at about 9% more per contact.

**Halden:** 14 of the 23 organisations with records responded. Three had reverted: hospitality, retail and a marketing agency. The 11 that continued show +11.8% per actual hour, presented explicitly as an upper bound for organisations that are survivors twice over.

**Earlier claims:**
- The "entirely an artifact" claim fails against a randomised, record-based, log-measured, two-year estimate.
- The meta-analysis's "no decay" rested on four long-follow-up studies that were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours.

The arithmetic checks out:
- 0.966/0.89 gives +8.5%, and 0.966/0.88 gives +9.8%.
- For Halden, 34.9/40.3 is −13.4%, and 96.8/86.6 gives +11.8%.

## Overall weight

This is good work, and it does what the earlier reports promised:

- It tests the three open questions under a protocol registered before the outcomes existed.
- It adds the stricter hours measure.
- It reports pre-period meeting data, which settles the baseline-imbalance concern I raised about the nine-month figures (7.4 v 7.2 hours).
- It treats its own Halden subset honestly.

Its finding that the meta-analysis's four long-follow-up studies were all uncontrolled and used scheduled hours confirms the suspicion I raised last time: those studies couldn't show anything about decay.

The main results deserve the weight given to them. The per-hour gain survives at two years under the strictest measures yet. Output per employee runs slightly below control. Wellbeing gains persist under randomisation, which is the first design-robust evidence on that point.

## Where it slips

**1. The control-office meeting audit contaminates the comparison, and that probably accounts for part of the apparent decay.**
- From month 15, two of the seven control offices cut meetings and gained about 4% per hour. That raises the control average by roughly 1 point (2/7 × 4.1%).
- The treatment–control gap shrinks by about that much. The like-for-like decline was about 2.7 points (12.5 → 9.8), so a third or more of it may come from the controls improving, not from the treated offices fading.

The report presents the audit as supporting evidence for the meetings mechanism, which is reasonable. But it doesn't note that the same event biases the main estimate. A sensitivity analysis that drops those two offices, or that ends the comparison at month 15, would show how much of the "decline" is contamination.

**2. The decline is asserted more firmly than the evidence allows.**
- The summary compares 12.5% (timesheets) with 8.5% (logs), which are different measures. The like-for-like change is 12.5% to 9.8%.
- The intervals overlap heavily (+6.9 to +18.4 at nine months; +4.6 to +15.2 at 24 months), and no test of the difference is reported, though one is easy with the same offices.
- With contamination added, "declined by about a quarter" should read "may have declined modestly".

The report is right that the meta-analysis's "no decay" was unsupported. But this trial doesn't establish decay either; it rules out decay *to zero*.

**3. It's unclear what the system logs measure, and that matters for both the hours correction and the mediation.**
"Active log-in time on the case-management system" sounds like time spent working *on cases*. If so:
- It excludes meetings, so it isn't a total-hours measure. Calling it "stricter" than timesheets would then be misleading; it measures something different.
- The mediation model becomes hard to read. Meeting time largely falls outside the denominator, so cutting meetings would raise output per log-hour only indirectly, for example through fewer interruptions, and not by freeing hours.

The report should state whether log time covers meetings and other work done off the system, and give the baseline levels, not just the percentage change.

**4. The mediation results are described in causal terms stronger than the design supports.**
- **Randomised:** the effect of treatment on meetings.
- **Not randomised:** the link from meetings to output, which comes from variation across offices. Offices that cut meetings most may also have better managers.
- The limitations admit this. But the summary says the analysis "confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47%", and that language is too strong.
- "A larger sample of office-months" also raises a question. The unit of randomisation is the office, and there are 14. Office-months aren't independent. If the confidence intervals don't account for clustering by office, they are too narrow. A 28–66% interval from 14 clusters looks tight.

"Survives a registered test" is accurate. "Accounts for" should be "is consistent with accounting for".

**5. A reversion in discretionary work is grouped under coverage.**
The summary says all three Halden reversions had "client-facing or coverage obligations". The marketing agency reverted over client deadlines. That is discretionary work in the meta-analysis's coding, and it is the first sign that deadline-driven discretionary work can also fail. One organisation proves little, but it should be reported as an exception to the work-type split, not absorbed into it.

Nine of the 23 organisations didn't respond, and nothing is said about them. If non-responders were more likely to have reverted, the reversion rate is understated.

## A correction to my own earlier reasoning

At nine months, I worked out that if meetings produce no output, the 3.3-hour meeting cut could account for "most" of the per-hour gain. The registered estimate is 47%.

At 24 months, the same simple accounting would attribute essentially *all* of the gain to meetings. Treated non-meeting time fell about as much as output did, roughly 3.5% each. That rests on two assumptions:
- that log hours represent total hours, which point 3 calls into question;
- that meetings produce nothing.

The mediation estimate is the better evidence. The gap between the two suggests meetings had some value, or that my accounting used the wrong denominator. Either way, my earlier "most of it" overstated the case.

## Where the evidence now stands

| Question | After the meta-analysis | Now |
|---|---|---|
| Per-hour gain, credible designs | ~8–10% | ~8.5–10% at two years in the best single trial. Consistent with the meta-analysis. |
| Per-worker output, discretionary work | Small loss, ~3% | ~−3% (CI includes zero); two sources agree |
| Durability | Open, leaning durable | Persists to 24 months in one setting, at the same or slightly lower size. How much it decays is open (contamination, untested difference). |
| Coverage-bound work | Settled: ~9% fall | Settled further: a county ended its arm; restoring service would cost about 9% more per contact |
| Mechanism | Open | Meetings are a substantial pathway (roughly half, provisionally), fatigue a smaller one. A third is unexplained. |
| Is the hours cut necessary? | Not asked | Open, and now the key question. Can meeting reform without a shorter week capture much of the gain? Two contaminated control offices hint yes; a reorganisation-only arm would answer it. |
| Wellbeing and retention | Consistent direction, design-adjusted size unknown | Established in one randomised setting at two years |

The literature has moved from asking whether shorter hours raise productivity to asking how much of the gain comes from the shorter week itself and how much from reorganisation that the shorter week forces. That is what an employer most needs to know, and no study yet answers it.

I can draft a note to the authors on points 1–4, or a two-page synthesis of all five documents for a non-specialist reader.
